item.dc:creator: Curiositry
item.content:encoded:
I drink caffeine. Like, a lot of caffeine. I have for a long time. Every once in a while I go on a ten-day caffeine fast to prune back my adenosine receptors, and when I start drinking coffee and yerba mate again, a tablespoon at a time, I think, wow, this is strong stuff!, and it’s a whole experience.

[ Skip to how to have whole experience without fasting. ]

But most days, after the first few sips of my cup of {coffee, yerba mate, pu-erh}, I bring it to my desk. I no longer consciously drink it, but as I work, the level goes down, and occasionally I catch myself holding the cup to my lips and making gulping sounds.

The other main time I drink tea and coffee is while visiting with people, which is more conscious, but only slightly.

Last month, I tried an experiment. I thought of caffeine as Nitro, and made a rule that I was only allowed to burn Nitro while the car was pointed in the right direction. So, I could take sips of caffeine while I was: doing nothing, going for a walk, sitting out-of-doors, reading a paper book, writing, working out, visiting. But I was not allowed to drink caffeine while surfing the internet, doing promotions and marketing, responding to emails, checking stats, or otherwise in my normal haze of low-value, life-sapping activities.

What happened is I realized why I like caffeine so much.

One day, I sat for somewhere between half and hour and an hour, in a comfortable chair by the woodstove, doing nothing, and nursing a large and very strong cup of coffee.

I am one of those people who wakes up impossibly groggy, almost every morning.

As I sipped my coffee, I could feel the grogginess being banished, more clearly than I ever have. And then, I could feel it being replaced with the sort of buzzing feeling that caffeine gives: and specifically, the sort of flushed, excited, go-getter version of the caffeine high that is unique to coffee.

I’m not a stranger to the feeling of having had too much caffeine: the tight feeling in the chest, the shaking, the sweating, the dry mouth, sometimes even heart palpitations. But this was different. Because I got to feel the good part, just before the too-much point, with a vividness that is usually reserved for when I overdo it. Glorious!

This is something that’s best tried on one of those vanishingly-rare Sunday mornings when the house is quiet, and it somehow feels like there’s nothing that needs to be done, and nothing, even, that I want to get done, and the day stretches before me, and time has the feeling of molasses.

But that’s a lot to ask. Even if you don’t have an hour to devote to it, I highly recommend trying some version of this. Queue up the amount of caffeine you usually drink in the course of one morning (ideally in a single cup of unusually good coffee). Sit somewhere comfortable where there isn’t human chatter. And then slowly, slowly drink the caffeine, while doing something even less productive than meditation, and feel what it does to you.

item.title: A Yes Person’s Guide to Saying No
item.description: I've always been an enthusiastic person. I like to jump from one project to the next (literally running, when possible) with my knobs turned to 11. I tend to do well on relatively short action cycles; getting started on (and being ready to move on from)
item.dc:creator: Immanuel
item.content:encoded:
I've always been an enthusiastic person. I like to jump from one project to the next (literally running, when possible) with my knobs turned to 11. I tend to do well on relatively short action cycles; getting started on (and being ready to move on from) tasks sooner than my more methodical peers. I like to jump in with both feet. And I like to say yes! when people ask me to do things, or collaborate on projects. This is partly because I genuinely like doing things, partly because I like to support well-intentioned projects, and partly because I want to be a generous person — someone who who helps out, pitches in, and, when reasonable, says yes rather than no. These things have gotten me in a lot of good places, brought me enjoyment (and plenty of hard work!), and in general I'm grateful for the results.

However, I've read the books. I've followed the blogs. And one thing they agree on: you need to be able to say no. In order to have your best effect in the world, you need to be able to choose (to a reasonable extent, at least) what your energy and attention goes on. This is vital. Otherwise, a great person with the best intentions can get side-tracked. They can end up using their life-force on projects that don't line up with their goals and aspirations, don't tap their unique skills, and don't contribute to the rest of the world in as meaningful a way as they could.

This being the case, how do we remain open and generous, be willing to say yes to people and help them out, while also being able to choose what we focus on so that our efforts are cumulative, and work towards the best possible overall outcome? This has been a tricky project for me. Below are some observations and techniques I've found helpful.

Create a Personal Hierarchy of Priorities:
This helps me choose what projects are important to me, how to prioritize my time, and what things line up well with my overall life roadmap. This can be something like: family → business → friends → volunteering. Or any other designation that you have decided on. The premise is that one thing takes priority over the next. This means if an opportunity comes up that's on a lower rung you have a simple yes/no choice on whether to accept it or not: if it conflicts with something you've placed on a higher rung of your hierarchy of priorities, the answer is no, but if it doesn't seem to be conflicting with anything higher up the ladder, that you can go ahead and say yes.

Separate out the Reasons:
I find it can be helpful to separate out the reasons why I might want to say yes or no to a specific request. Sometimes I'll get a job offer or request from a friend. The job part of the offer will clearly be a no, but I would still like to help out the friend, be kind, or even visit with them. Sometimes the offer will be a combination of a request to hang out, help them, and do a "job". And this isn't usually a happy combination for me. In these cases, I try to separate out the request, follow through with the part that's mutually beneficial, and decline the part that's not a good match. An example of this would be: if a friend asks me to come do a job for them (paid) and hang out while I'm at it or have tea. I would likely respond with an grateful yes to the hanging out part, and a (hopefully) graceful no to the job part, unless it was something that actually lined up with my professional skills. I might try and redirect the job part of the offer to some more suitable candidate by providing a good recommendation for someone else to hire. It's great to know a collection of good people who offer services such as tech support, proof-reading, website help, or anything else you can do, and people tend to ask you to do, but you're not actually very good at, and or don't enjoy. In my opinion this is much better than struggling though the job, not wanting to, just to be nice, while the other person thinks they're doing a nice thing by offering it to me. Another option in this situation is to take on the job purely as a favour. This means I do employ my professional skills on their behalf, but don't accept any monetary exchange, and treat it as a favour for the acquaintance, or maybe in exchange for their help in some other area.

Exit the Vortex:
I've written about this technique before as a way to avoid impulse purchases. The tactic is to simply force myself to exit the gravitational pull of whatever the thing is (ie: get outside the store if it's in a store) before making any decisions about it. Not only does this protect against getting sold things I don't want or need (on the phone or in person), in the literal sense, it also works for avoiding getting talked into things, or getting reeled in by fascinating individuals for non-commercial purposes. When making decisions on possible commitments, I try to exit the vortex and make my decision on neutral ground.

The Three Second Rule:
In my experience, this is a good way to curb my knee-jerk habit of saying yes to things regardless of if I want to, or it's a good idea – something I've been trying to get better at. The strategy is: when asked about something, even if it feels awkward, take the time to think about it for three seconds before responding yes or no.

"Let Me Think About It"
Similar to exiting the vortex, and the three second rule, this is a way to let the pressure off enough that you can make the right decision. For those of us who like to respond to all inquiries in a timely manner, this is a good way to acknowledge the offer right away, while gracefully delaying the actual decision a little. I find this approach useful especially with offers and requests that come in by email. The tactic is to respond right away with a short message expressing my gratitude for the offer and saying that I'll consider it and let them know shortly. This means the other person knows you received their message, and that you're giving some respectful consideration. It also indicates that I take my commitments seriously and just because they ask me to do something doesn't mean I'm necessarily going to automatically do it for them. I think it helps to remind myself of this also.

If it's not a definite yes, then it should definitely be a no:
For projects that are going to take a lot of time and energy, it's worth making sure they are really lined up with your aims. Otherwise, they will be pulling energy away from what you actually want to be focusing and working on. Sometimes a good test for this is asking yourself "is this project something I definitely want to take on?" If it's not a clear yes, it's likely a bit lukewarm, and therefor might not be something to dive into. This is a tactic I incorporated after reading High Performance Habits, one of my all-time favourite books.

How many opportunities to turn down scales with how busy you are. If you have better opportunities available, no makes perfect sense. But when you're expanding into a new field, sometimes taking even so-so opportunities, and doing an amazing job, leads to new, better opportunities.

Everything I Say Yes to, Means I'm Saying No to Something Else:
This can be a depressing outlook, especially for the type of person who likes to do and be part of everything, but it's also kind of true. Any time I'm working on one project, there are probably at least two or three equally worthy projects that I could be working on with the same slot of time and energy. Since this is the case, it's good to remember that it is the case, especially when I'm about to commit to something.

Get a Wingman:
It can be helpful to have a more methodical/conservative friend or buddy you can run ideas by before committing to them. They can provide a useful (if sometimes annoying) perspective or second opinion on if you should say yes or no. This is also a good idea with estimates. Some of us tend to chronically underestimate, and an external perspective can help pull the wool off our heads on how long something is going to take.

Conclusion: I hope this article is helpful, and not too depressing, for any other yes people out there who like to take on the whole world at once, but also want to avoid being dragged from one commitment to another, or pulled in so many different directions at once that the quality of your work suffers. And hopefully it helps you select and work on your unique highest-value contribution to the world, rather than whatever random thing someone asks you to do for them, which someone else could do just as well or better than you could.

Further Reading:
A Better Way to Say No
High Performance Habits
7 Habits of Highly Effective People

item.title: The Command Line as Franken-REPL
item.description: Learning to thrive in the Mos Eisley cantina
item.dc:creator: Curiositry
item.content:encoded:
[ Dear unix nerds: I am about to blow smoke. I’m so excited I might be totally wrong. ]

As I have belabored before, I’ve been using Linux since I was a babe, and have gradually become comfortable doing most tasks from the command line.

But my mental model of what the command line is has always been wrong!

The four stages of understanding:

1. The command line is scary

Okay, sure, the command line is scary. We don’t talk about that. Because the command line is scary in the same way fire or the ocean or a chainsaw or a knife or an irate grandma is scary: it’s scary because it can do things, and we don’t like all the things it can do, even though we value most of them.

These things are mostly scary because we don’t know what they can do, and what they will do. There are two approaches: stay away, or try to understand them. We have already chosen the second.

2. The command line is a text interface for running programs

Also technically true. This is where I was stuck for a long time.

Type command. Read output. Google error. Try again. You put one thing in and you get one thing out: like a mailbox for my computer’s innards.

3. The command line is a {Shell,Bash,Fish,Zsh,Nushell,Oils} interpreter

Also true! Not only true, useful. It’s easy to forget that an entire b-grade programming language is at your finger tips at all times, because you’re living in its read–eval–print loop (REPL).

4. The command line is an everything-REPL!

So, technically, #3 is maybe the most accurate. But, because of the way Bash (and other shell scripting languages) work, this model is more useful. Because, in bash, you don’t need some ugly spawn/exec/eval syntax to run something that isn’t bash: you just run it using the name of the executable. Rather than having to send registered mail with a formal request bearing your letterhead, you can just shout Dave! What’s 12 times 6?, and he answers.

This seems like a small difference, but it’s not.

This turns your shell into an interactive REPL … for all programming languages. (As long as I don’t mind bashing my head against all the ways that bash is weird and bad.)

Not only can you use any programming language from bash, without elaborate spawning rituals, but all your scripts and abbreviations also have first class support, and, most importantly, so do the coreutils. Once you’ve mastered them, you rarely need more than the coreutils.

I used to think of commands as commands, as programs. But take a look at cat file.part1 file.part2. Is that a program? No, no, no! That’s a function. In bash, programs are functions. All the coreutils feel almost as native as the bash builtins.

(And instead of an SQL database, you have the filesystem. Which, incidentally, is where the scripts are stored, making the whole thing a heady Lisp-like situation.)

Every little utility shell script you write becomes another function in your computer-wide REPL, that you can re-use.

Your entire computer is deliciously scriptable, once you realize that there is no boundary between the program and the computer.

A reader said I should probably end on a high note, with the fact that it’s “hopelessly ugly and unusually dangerous”. In his own words:

the command line is the most powerful and inscrutable programming context, with zero safeguards and total power over your system. But, it’s pretty sweet!

item.title: A Local AI Stack for Language Learning
item.description: Immersive, pretty fun, and you learn $OTHER_SUBJECT at the same time
item.dc:creator: Curiositry
item.content:encoded:
I have written before about my lazy and largely unsuccessful journey to become a polyglot. (TL;DR Duolingo doesn’t work, LanguageTransfer is cool, and the only thing that makes a difference is crossing the cringe minefield and talking to people before you know how to talk to people.)

I stand by what I said, but talking to people is, like, a lot of work and super embarrassing. Here’s a way to practice your foreign language of choice that doesn’t require talking to people, in a way that feels a lot like talking to people, because you are talking, and getting natural language replies, and you have to understand what’s going on.

The system has two parts (in the future, I’d like it to have three):

  1. Speak at your local AI in a foreign language
  2. It replies in text in the foreign language, correcting your grammar
  3. (Coming soon: Moonshine STT reads it aloud)

Part I: Dictation in your target language, with Handy

I wrote about how handy Handy is. But what’s extra handy about it, is that it’s multilingual, and it can even translate between languages!

Although it’s forgiving, you do have to get the pronunciation close enough for it to be unambiguous.

  1. Install Handy (or any other equally good multilingual dictation tool)
  2. In the settings, change the model to Canary 180M Flash. I have found that this is the sweet spot for a speech-to-text model that runs in near realtime, and is multi lingual and accurate enough for the purpose. If your target language isn’t supported by Canary 180M Flash, or you have a more or less powerful laptop, the optimal model might be different.
  3. Set the language (in the General tab) to your target language; in my case, Spanish.
  4. Set a hotkey, if you haven’t already.

Test this set up by opening a text editor, pressing your dictation hotkey, and transcribing some foreign language speech.

Part II: The Language Teacher, Powered by Llama.cpp + Qwen

Follow my tutorial to install Llama.cpp and Qwen. For language learning, any modern model will probably work okay. So you could use Ollama, or Jan.ai, or (if you wanna be uncool) some free vaguely-privacy-respecting cloud model like Brave AI or Lumo.

Putting it all together!

Fire up Handy so that’s running in your tray, and start your llama.cpp server (or AI chat of choice).

The third ingredient is the prompt. We don’t want to just say, talk to me. Because it’s much more fun to try to learn something we want to learn anyway. The foreign language is just something that’s getting between us and what we want, so we won’t get obsessed with grammar, we will focus on understanding, and being understood!

Despite running several math websites, I kind of suck at doing arithmetic in my head. I also … wasn’t good at counting in Spanish. So my starting prompt was this:

I’m learning Spanish. Please have a conversation with me in the language. I want to learn basic mathematics, especially how to do arithmetic (multiplication etc) in my head and on paper without a calculator. Teach them to me step by step, in Spanish, with quizzes and exercises. I will reply in Spanish. Below your response in Spanish, include corrections to my Spanish usage, and a brief English translation of what you said (esp any difficult words that haven’t been used in the conversation before)

Working Around Context Length Limitations

Depending on how powerful your system is, there likely won’t be enough context length available for more than a few near-realtime conversations. My solution is a prompt specifically for saving the current state of the lessons, so I can start where I left off in a fresh session:

Write a careful, thoughtful lesson plan, including what we have covered so far, all the way through to fluency in both Spanish and Math. Include a list of words that have been introduced and I have learned to use, as well as a list of key terms and mathematical concepts that I have not yet learned. Make it concrete, so it is easy to start where we left off, even without access to the chat history, without repeating or skipping over any material. The idea is that each session, I paste the lesson plan as the starting prompt, do a bunch, and then have the AI update the lesson plan, and start fresh the next day, starting from just the lesson plan.

But we’re missing the best part!

You’re right. The hardest part of learning Spanish isn’t speaking it, it’s understanding it. People speak so fast, and all the words run together!

For a long time, I’ve been trying to get a full 3-part system working, without luck. I have at last succeeded! (It’s still a bit janky.)

Stay tuned for the sequel to this post, Immersive, Fully Local Speech-to-Speech Foreign Language Learning in ~30 lines of Bash.

item.title: Curiosity Traps
item.description: On reverse honeypots, rewarding close attention, and finding your people
item.dc:creator: Curiositry
item.content:encoded:
In computing, honeypots attract bad actors into interacting with a system.

As usual, this principle can be reversed. You can deliberately put out some kind of intellectual honey that will attract good actors instead, and lead to joyful serendipity.

If you wear a shirt that says, “Dyslexics are teople poo”, that attracts one kind of conversation; a CERN standard model tee attracts another (in my case: “what’s it mean?”, “dunno”, the end.). The examples are endless – trail race swag attracts conversations with fellow trail runners; wearing something handmade gets the attention of other crafters – but conversations started by conversation pieces aren’t usually that deep or well-targeted.

Conversation pieces are decent at starting conversations, but we don’t see that many people face-to-face (well, I don’t!), so there’s a limit to how specific you can make the reference, and still meet people who get it.

Henrik Karlsson (are you tired of me referencing Henrik Karlsson yet?) articulated the idea that a blog, or any public collection of work, is a way of passively collecting a network of interesting people that are unusually well-matched with your interests, without having to go to hundreds of speed-networking events in a nerdy tee shirt.

This seems true. I’ve met a lot of interesting people by putting things out on the internet. But this, like most worthwhile things, can be fractal.

First you go in public, then you wear a conversation piece, then you leave “handles” and “doorknobs” in your answers to the basic questions, creating a choose-your-own adventure for your conversation partner.

First you make stuff, then you put it on the internet. If you stop here, you’re missing out! That’s like going out in public – with airpods in, and staring at the ground. The next step is to put lots of links to your contact form or email, and explicitly ask for feedback, and make it easy for people to say hello.

Each post is a hook for a different conversation, with a different kind of person. Each post has a chance of pushing a reader over the activation energy threshold to start a conversation. Posts are, also, cumulative. Someone might read for years, and then write in to discuss draining pasta without a colander.

(Other people might subscribe, and then realize, oh, that’s not actually an $X blog, it’s a kitchen sink blog, and I’m only interested in 1/10th of the things they write about. Bye! If you have to pay to send emails, this is actually a good thing. They can still read your posts about $X when they bubble up in the $X communities they hang out in.)

But within a blog, you can also place Easter eggs that target sub-segments of your readers.

[ SPOILERS FOR WAITBUTWHY READERS AHEAD ]

I’m old enough to remember the turtle in Wait Buy Why’s footer, which went to a page that said “You clicked the turtle”. This is a classic curiosity trap. The people who end up on that page are a small segment of their most engaged and curious readers.

I don’t see the turtle in the footer anymore. Only today did I discover that it’s turtles all the way down. The turtle page has a turtle that goes to another page, that has a smaller turtle that goes to another page that claims “You Win” but actually has a tiny turtle that goes to I actually can’t believe you, which has a giraffe that goes to Tim Urban’s old blog. Maybe it also has a pico-turtle that I missed.

This was probably what gave me the idea for using the interrobang as the icon for my /intractable page. And the whole idea of the intractable page is that it’s an entire box of doorknobs. Whether or not they found it via the tiny interrobang in the footer, nifty people have written in as a result of that page, and I consider it a success.

I’d like to cook up a game that writers and anyone else can play, of burying things in their work that only the most attentive people will notice, as a way of incentivizing that kind of close attention.

Then I thought, wait, that game has already been invented! It’s called life.

This is also, generally, how art works. (Adam Mastroianni has a great post about art that rewards close attention.)

But even if the universe already works this way, and art already works this way, we can turn up the gain, and create a subsubgame within the subgame within the game, where the rules and rewards are made more clear and immediate.

Wait But Why gives one simple example: a treasure hunt with the first clue hidden. Footnotes are another.[1] For anything put in public, there is a distribution of how deeply people engage with it. For public art: ignore, glance over, stop and look, go over and look, climb/look-up-on-the-internet/copy/vandalize/destroy.[2]

One of the tricky things about creating layered art is how to make it work on all levels. (Henrik thinks this isn’t necessary; I somewhat disagree.) If you put the heavy math in the main text, mathphobes stop reading. Basically, everyone is looking for an excuse to stop reading, so the more tangents and puzzles you include, the fewer people make it to the end. [3] Different people have different goals about how widely they want to appeal, and how many people they are willing to drive off, in order to engage their ideal readers.

Footnotes[4], inside jokes that
don’t
disrupt
the flow
of reading,
and links to explainers of unfamiliar concepts are all ways of catering to different audiences in the same piece, the same way that cafés offer both dine-in and takeout.

An obvious example is text holding invisible significance. Cyphers are fun, but they tend to be fun in the same way that picking very small berries is fun. It’s fun at first, but only as a novelty, because the payoff doesn’t justify the effort. They often feel like a tangent.

Many famous people make it possible, but difficult, to find their contact info 🔒. This is another example of rewarding the most engaged readers. And tech companies often put their job postings in the sourcecode, or print them to the browser console, as a way of filtering candidates. [5]

Another problem with the whole concept of curiosity traps is that sometimes the people who engage most deeply are obsessed weirdos, rather than people with unusually aligned interests. This is more a problem for people who are famous personalities. In my experience, the people who write in to obscure blogs tend to be unusual in a good way.

Easter Eggs and gimmicks are fun, and worth including. But after trying to write an article about these artificial curiosity traps, I have realized that the best curiosity traps emerge naturally. If you write from concrete experience, and you publish a lot, people will notice the details. Because I was once a designer, every time I go to a website made by a designer, even if the layout is very plain, there’s something hard to place, but recognizably designed, that I appreciate. This applies everywhere: we notice when other people care about the things we care about. And when we notice that someone else cares about very similar things[6], it feels like meeting a friend we haven’t met yet.

  1. You clicked the footnote! You are special. Now we are stuck in here together. If my footnote script supported nested footnotes, we could keep going all day! [7] ↩︎

  2. Most public art disappoints me, but the pretzeled balsa rubber band aeroplane in Stanley Park – er, I mean, cough Aerodynamic Forms in Space cough — has always tickled me.[8] ↩︎

  3. Case study: someone who is fairly close to my ideal reader read a draft of this essay. He pointed out design flaws with my blog, typos, and “unfinished thoughts”, and generally engaged deeply with the text[10] (even opening the devtools to inspect the footnote implementation), yet missed every single easter egg, and concluded that the last paragraph was his favourite, because:

    I don’t really engage with the internet as a social… as a way of meeting people. I mostly engage in other ways that are mostly fairly mercantile: to learn or disseminate knowledge, in an urgent way.
    This is a valuable reader who I would like to keep, even if they miss all my curiosity traps, so it’s important to make the traps subtle enough that they don’t slow down and irritate readers of this type, who aren’t interested in solving silly puzzles, and just want to get to the point, if there is one. ↩︎

  4. I mostly use footnotes like this: 1) move the weakest and most digressive parts to footnotes, then 2) realize they aren’t needed, and 3) delete the footnotes. This one got missed. ↩︎

  5. Google is famous for their billboard problem: . ↩︎

  6. A recent example: https://stevekrouse.com/readme ↩︎

  7. https://dn721608.ca.archive.org/0/items/a-night-at-the-opera-1935-HD/A Night at the Opera.mp4#t=250,285 ↩︎

  8. I am sorry that I spoiled both of these in the post about how I figured out how to deeplink :( [9] ↩︎

  9. Okay, if you're here you are very special, having figured out that I deliberately left my nested footnotes broken so you would have to view source or use reader mode. (In my markdown file, this footnote has the id #final-boss.) You are also probably the kind of person who would definitely click on "Don't click this link!". Also, by now you may agree with me that puzzles and cyphers, without an adequate payoff, are an annoying tangent. ↩︎

  10. The same reader recommended the subtitle "honeypot for pooh bear". Does this not throw doubt on everything else he said? Unless, of course, it was a test to make sure I wasn't shunting the brain and blindly following all his suggestions. ↩︎

item.dc:creator: Curiositry
item.content:encoded:
Although I’m a semi-professional musician, most days, I listen to far less music than my friends. I generally work in silence, cook in silence, run in silence. When I do listen to music, usually in the evening, I give it my full attention. Everybody is different, and different kinds of music work well in different contexts, but I can’t help feeling that anyone who doesn’t sometimes listen to music the way I do is missing out.

The way I do it is like this: lying on my back, wearing headphones, from an MP3 player rather than a smartphone/computer, usually in the evening in bed, after I have put down my book, but before I will be able to sleep, with, if possible, nothing on my mind.

Most good music has a story. Sometimes, a song can have multiple stories, depending on what you bring to it. I like to place my mind on the melody, the the needle of a record player placed in the groove, and stick to it and see where it takes me. Melodies are stories, and I’m a sucker for stories. Song lyrics are also often stories. And a good story isn’t just the story that’s told: it’s all the other stories that have the same shape, and the story of the negative space of what isn’t said.

Most stories are like fractals, and implied in the scale perceived is the resonance of the micro and macrocosm that have the same shape.

But even if you aren’t interested in stories, lyrical or melodic, there are good reasons to listen this way. There’s so much to hear in a good song! There’s no way I could absorb it all in one pass through, or with it on in the background. I can listen to a song dozens or hundreds of times, and still be surprised when I really hear one part for the first time.

(For more on this theme, see The Joy of Selective Attention.)

I have my music collection organized into four parts: the stuff I’m tired of or never really liked (which stays in cold storage), an “inbox” of things to check out, a collection of songs that do something really well that I could learn from but which aren’t really my thing, and then my active collection of songs that have turned my crank before. I usually start from the inbox (explore), and end with my main collection, or a specific playlist from my main collection (exploit).

If there’s a new album from an artist I like, I try to listen to it in one sitting, without multi-tasking. I still remember the day I did that with Oliver Schroer’s Hymns and Hers, and David Francey’s The Breath Between, and in my rap phase, The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill — and with Leonard Bernstein’s version of Beethoven’s 9th Symphony, which I later heard wasn’t even the best one — and was richly rewarded.

I like using playlists, but depending on how the day has gone, which songs affect me varies widely. But I can usually tell which song I need to hear within a few seconds. So I find that a playlist of a few hundred songs, all of which I have moved or inspired or amused me sometimes, is the right balance of being able to find the song for the moment, without spending too much time clicking fast-forward. And there’s something about (pseudo) randomness delivering me musical deliverance that I like. Sometimes, the song that would be just the thing is one that I wouldn’t have chosen, if the choice had been mine.

Although I prefer to listen to songs that are good (according to me) through-and-through, there are songs that I listen to just for one word. I’m a connoisseur of grittily-enunicated filler “yeah”s. The rest of the lyrics might be dumb, but the sound of that careless British “yeah” in The Cars’ Just What I Wanted is hard to beat. (Ziggy Marley’s Circle of Peace also features an exceptional yeah.) I’ll also listen to music for the electric guitar tone (I have yet to hear an overdrive crunchier than Green Day), or the bass solo (Bakithi Kumalo on You Can Call Me Al, the breakdown in Miracles out of Nowhere), or the snare tone, or the storytelling (Dispatch’s The General), or fragments of poetry (“with his eyes he said he loved them” in Circles Around the Sun), or the associations with a particular time of my life

Listening to music like this is less like sitting in front of a TV, and more like a choose-your-own-adventure game. It requires sustained attention. I know it’s an active process, because if I’m really tired, to the point that my mind wanders and my heart feels sodden, then it doesn’t work. If I don’t bring anything to it, I don’t get anything from it. Such is life.

item.title: Did you know you can link to a timestamp in a plain video file?
item.description: TIL how to deeplink all the things
item.dc:creator: Curiositry
item.content:encoded:
I have written before about how to link to a specific segment of a youtube video, and how to link to specific words or paragraphs within a webpage. I even knew, vaguely, that you could link to pages of PDFs. But, all in the course of a normal workday researching a blogpost, I found myself wanting reference a specific ~30 second chunk of a Marx Brothers movie from 1935, and the last page of a PDF about a piece of public art.

The PDF was easy, using the #page=n syntax.

As for the scene from the movie: nobody had clipped that specific part out and put it on YouTube – in fact, I didn’t even find the scene I was looking for – but I did find an mp4 on the Internet Archive with a scene that fit my requirements.

It turns out, you can link to a specific segment of an Mp4, too!

This is thanks to the Media Fragments URI 1.0 (basic) W3C spec recommendation from 2012. According to CanIUse, media fragments are supported by all major browsers (97-99% of users).

The syntax is nice: https://example.com/video.mp4#t=startTime,endTime

(Notice that it’s a pound/hash symbol. I always wanted to use a question mark.)

An actual example:

https://dn721608.ca.archive.org/0/items/a-night-at-the-opera-1935-HD/A Night at the Opera.mp4#t=250,285

What’s especially cool is that you can play from (only specify start time):

https://dn721608.ca.archive.org/0/items/a-night-at-the-opera-1935-HD/A Night at the Opera.mp4#t=250,

…play to (only specify end time):

https://dn721608.ca.archive.org/0/items/a-night-at-the-opera-1935-HD/A%20Night%20at%20the%20Opera.mp4#t=,285

…or play a segment (specify both start and end time):

https://dn721608.ca.archive.org/0/items/a-night-at-the-opera-1935-HD/A Night at the Opera.mp4#t=250,285

And, you can format the timestamps as seconds by using a plain integer, or as hh:mm or hh:mm:ss . (You can also, weirdly, use h:mm:ss format.) This is generally more convenient, since most video players reference current playhead location using hours and minutes, not seconds.

https://www.autodidacts.io/content/media/2026/09/2026-09-24-copy-all-tabs-urls-firefox.webm#t=00:00:04,00:00:05

And it works for audio files too?!

Look at how much good stuff I have been missing out on!

While we are at it: you can also crop SVGs. I didn’t know that, either.

At this point I’m just duplicating the excellent, slightly more intimidating article on MDN, so if you like what you’ve heard, go read it.

Even better, try the playgrounds: link, link!

item.title: How to copy URLs of multiple Firefox tabs without installing an extension
item.description: It’s easy, once you know you can
item.dc:creator: Curiositry
item.content:encoded:
Once upon a time, I ran across an experimental project called TabFS, which mounts browser tabs as a filesystem. This seemed like such a cool idea! Ever since, I have wanted a way to interact with tabs programmatically. But the main thing I’ve wanted to do is be able to grab the URLs of some or all of my open tabs, and paste them into a text file.

Each time I have looked into this before, it hasn’t been possible without installing an extension. And I don’t like installing extensions.

I often have text files of URLs, one per line, related to some project. Often I want to be able to open them all in Firefox (easy in Helix editor with %s\n<ret>xgf [1]) while I’m working on the project, close ones that aren’t relevant any longer and follow new leads, and then save the updated list when I’m done, without interacting with bookmarks (my graveyard for URLs that are “interesting” and “relevant” and I’m definitely never going to visit again).

Another common use-case is when I want to copy the URLs for a group of tabs and pass them to a script (in this case, my Ghost API markdown export script).

Today, I discovered that it’s not just possible, it’s easy! It looks like this feature was added in v152.0a1, 4 months ago.

  1. Select some tabs (right click on a tab, then click “Select all tabs”; or click on one tab, then shift click on another to select range, or ctrl click to cherry-pick individual tabs)
  2. Right click on tab, or open File menu
  3. Click “Share”
  4. Click “Copy n links”

Watch:


You can do steps 2-4 in one go by pressing (in sequence) Alt f h l

I want to be able to do everything with the keyboard. However, although you can cycle through tabs and move tabs with keybindings, weirdly, there doesn’t seem to be a Firefox keybinding for selecting tabs, or for opening the tab right click menu (Shift+F10 opens the page right click menu, even if tabs are selected and the mouse is hovering over a tab).

If you paste these tabs into a rich text field, they will be links with titles, but if you paste them into a plaintext editor, they will be plain URLs, one per line!

  1. % select buffer, s open split dialog, \n split delimiter, <ret>/Enter split selection on delimiter, x extend selections to whole line, gf (g)oto (f)ile, which opens URLs in the browser ↩︎

item.title: How wise do our mentors need to be?
item.description:

item.dc:creator: Curiositry
item.content:encoded:
[ In Iteration, I wrote about the mistake of demanding painting lessons from van Gogh. This essay tugs upon on the same thread. ]

There's an old saying that in order to teach a dog, you just have to be smarter than the dog. As with most proverbs, I think there's some truth there, but it's not that simple.

  1. If the path is straight, to lead the dog, you just have to be ahead of the dog.
  2. If the path is non-linear, mentorship from someone just ahead of you might help, but also might lead you on unnecessary detours.

As far as I can tell, approximately nobody's development follows a straight line toward a destination.

Even with simple skills, like, say, swimming a certain distance faster, following the advice of someone better than you might have suboptimal results. Because it's possible to "improve" using naïve optimization that makes you better in the short run, but worse in the long run.

A slightly more advanced student might try to improve the floundering student's back crawl, since that's what they're using, poorly, and the coach is using more skillfully. But anyone with actual experience will try to figure out why the student can't breathe properly doing front crawl. First it will be slow, then it will be fast, which, in the long run, is much better than getting quick gains and then plateauing at a local optimum (very fast at a very slow stroke).

(A wiser mentor, even if they took a circuitous path, might, in hindsight, be able to see that the path they took isn't the best path. However, it's also possible that the shortest/fastest path is not the best one for a particular student, for reasons that are opaque even to the wise mentor. Perhaps, if the wise mentor were even wiser, they would see that the detours are, in this case, necessary. So, in the case of my illustration, a wiser wise mentor could have taken the direct route or the spiral route, and might recommend the route they took or the other route, depending on circumstances. However, as long as the game is in play, there's perhaps a limit to the knowledge of even the wisest of the wise.)

But getting a fancier coach isn't the whole answer, because of the problems I mentioned in Iteration: the scarcity of expert-time, expert-access, and expert-patience, as well as difficulty stepping down expert advice to a level that can be understood and applied by the student. (The difference between an expert and a teacher is, I suppose, whether the stepping-down is bundled with the expertise.)

My solution is, go ahead and learn from the person just ahead of you, but verify what you've learned with a true expert.

When I did my lifeguarding pre-requisite course, I found coaching from a more advanced student more helpful than coaching from the instructors. The advanced student had just learned what I was trying to learn. It was fresh, rather than muscle memory. The instructors would explain some new stroke: I’d try it, and it would totally fail to work. I'd watch the instructors do it, but they made it look so effortless I couldn't even tell what was going on. So I'd ask the more advanced student if he'd gotten it to work, and he'd say, yeah, by ignoring what the instructors said, and doing what felt intuitive. I managed to get the imperfect intuitive version to work, which got me from zero propulsion, to enough propulsion I could continue practicing the stroke without sinking.

If I continued to just do that version, I might end up with some bad habits. But from there, I could try to make it look more like what the instructors were doing, and then ask them, does this look right?

In the AI world, the cool kids often run cheap dumb models to do the grunt work, and smart expensive models to do the planning and the evaluation. In business, it's the same, with high paid people monitoring and correcting, and low paid people doing the work.

(As much as it pains me to suggest that the AI and business junkies are onto something, they are. But it's an idea they stole from the structure of the human brain and/or an ant colony, so we don't need to give them credit.)

We need multiple mentors, some far ahead of us, and some just ahead of us. That way, I can spend most of my time learning the practical details of the skill from the person just ahead of me, and then occasionally check in with the real expert, to make sure I'm going the right direction, and haven't ended up copying the intermediate student's flaws along with their skills.

item.title: Ode to Metadata
item.dc:creator: Curiositry
item.content:encoded:
The first thing I wrote when I started this essay was, "Written 2026-09-01." Then I wrote "Idea long before that". Then I opened my post ideas file and searched for "metadata", and found the line where I had written down the title for this essay, four years ago. Then I wrote "Idea and title 2022-07-30".

Does this sound tedious? It is tedious. But, it's worth it.

I have written before about how much I like dating. (No, no, not that kind of dating. ISO_8601 dating!) But my obsession with timestamps is just part of a broader belief in the long-term value of metadata.

Why save metadata? Briefly: because it's way easier to record data when it's fresh, than to have to piece it together later.

Additionally, I think that:

  1. We wildly overestimate our chance of remembering things.
  2. We often have no idea what will prove to be important.

We think, oh, that doesn't matter. Or, oh, I'll never forget that. But it does, and I will, and I'll only realize that it does after I have.

More likely, someone else will realize it does, long after I'm gone. And they'll be like me: wasting a non-profit's money and getting a headache trying to trace the provenance of obscure foreign-language manuscripts that were published under different titles in different languages.

What does this mean in practice? Here are some examples:

I write songs. When I write a song, I make sure to:

  1. record a memo of it
  2. write down the lyrics
  3. put the chords in the lyrics
  4. fill out a template with all kinds of boring stuff about it: the key, capo position, accompaniment, date started, date worked on, date finished, tempo.

At the time the song is fresh, it all seems a bit absurd. Am I really going to forget what instrument I play on a song that I wrote? A song that took me, probably, a day to six months to finish? Am I going to forget what key it's in? Forget what order the three chords go in?

Yes, yes I am. And years later, the drummer is going to forget he played drums, and try to play cello on it, and it will sound bad.

Some songwriters I know don't put the chords in their songs, or notate the key. They are the creative types that write in a cute little notebook, and haven't written custom software for managing their song catalogue. Then, years later, they try to play them, and discover that they have forgotten which order the three chords go in.

(Fun fact of interest of to almost nobody, because the Venn diagrams of "songwriter" and "nerd" have so little overlap: Regex can make adding chord notation to lyrics way faster.)

Also, lyrics will drift. Usually this is good. Unmemorable parts get dropped, just like with folk songs. But sometimes you want to go back to the first version, in case something good got left by the wayside.

Code comments are another obvious form of metadata:

I write a lot of infrequently used shell scripts. Some of them are meant to be run from a particular place, or as a step in a pipeline, or are full of known footguns that I haven't bothered to fix. It saves a lot of time to add a comment at the top with usage instructions, while I still remember how to run the script. Better yet, echo the usage instructions, and exit if the config is wrong.

I also think of logging as a form of metadata. As soon as something breaks, the first thing I do is add logging. So I've started by adding logging right at the beginning, so all I need to do when the software breaks is turn on the logging.

If you have gone to the dark side, I highly recommend that you record:

  • what model you used
  • if running locally: quantization, inference engine, and parameters
  • the prompt

The thing about vibecoding is that I don't understand it, so I don't remember it. This paper trail allows me to remember where I was on a project, if it gets shelved and then I try to come back to it.

If you're a writer, have a good schema for tracking different versions of things. Fancy people use git; I use numbers at the end of the filename. Title final-final-FINAL.doc does not count as "a good schema for tracking different versions of things".

Any time I write an email in a text editor, and then paste it into my email client before sending, and then tweak it in the email editor, I add a note to the text file NOT UP TO DATE. (Sometimes, I put CANONICAL VERSION in whatever is the up-to-date version of a document that lives multiple places, in different forms. This is, of course, fragile, but it's often better than nothing.)

When I scan papers, I pencil on them that they have been scanned (or, typed in), and the date.

Another reason to save metadata: to protect against lawsuits. Often, I write something, or write a song, and then notice a similarity to some other work. If I saved a good record of my process, I can cross-reference: had I read that article, or heard that song, before I started mine?

(Astute readers will notice that this won't actually protect me from lawsuits, though maybe it would help. But it will ease my conscience.)

Obviously, if you are into plagiarism, then you probably shouldn't save metadata, since it will make it easier for them to catch you!

Another kind of metadata is indexing metadata. It's not data about what, it's data about where: lightweight, easy-to-find data that points to heavy buried (meta)data somewhere else. Things like unreasonably long filenames, and notes about where the notes are.

What are the reasons not to save metadata?

  • It's slow
  • It takes up space
  • It's tedious
  • It's revealing

These are legitimate reasons, but in most cases, I think they are outweighed by the benefits.

Metadata adds the fourth dimension to your projects: their trajectory through time. It's much easier to steer something into the future if you know the path it took on its way to the present.
